notes.title: Start here: two real stories about progress that silently broke
notes.body:
This pack draws on three short documents in the `upskilling/` folder. Read them in this order:

1. **Case study 09** (`upskilling/case-studies/09-the-roadmap-as-data-and-stable-step-keys.md`). It tells the story: the curriculum lives in a JSON file, and every learner's saved ticks secretly depended on where each step sat in that file.
2. **Decision record 0001** (`upskilling/examples/decision-record-step-keys.md`). The same problem written up as a formal decision: the context, the five key options, the two migration options, what was chosen and what it costs.
3. **The postmortem** (`upskilling/examples/postmortem-strictmode-double-grade.md`). A separate bug: a timed-out drill question was graded twice in development under React's StrictMode.

While you read, keep the code open next to the guide: `app/src/lib/types.ts` (how a step key is built), `app/src/lib/progress.ts` (how saved progress is read and migrated) and `app/src/routes/DrillSession.tsx` (the countdown and the answer handler). The guides cite line numbers in those files; check each claim against the code rather than taking it on trust.

A useful habit for both stories: ask "what is stored, where, and what does it depend on?" Most of the questions in this pack come back to that.

excerpts.quote: Putting a curriculum in a JSON file instead of in code is an easy decision to agree with. This case is about the coupling it created without anyone choosing it: every learner's saved progress depended on the *position* of each step in that file. Three reviews found it independently. The fix is a good example of changing a key that is already stored in thousands of places you cannot reach.

readMore.why: The full story of the step-key change, with the reasons for each part of the key.
The formal decision record: options, decision and consequences.
The double-grade postmortem: timeline, root cause and action items.

notes.title: Why a key built from a position is fragile
notes.body:
A **progress key** is the string the app uses to remember "this learner finished this step". It is saved in the browser's `localStorage` and in exported progress files, so once it ships you cannot reach in and change it for every learner.

The first version built the key from the stage id, the module id and the step's **index** (its position in the module's list). That is unique and costs nothing, which is why it looked fine. The trouble is that a position describes *where* a step sits, not *what* it is. Before reading on, work out for yourself what an old saved key would point at after an author inserts, removes or reorders a step, and whether anything in the app would notice.

The guide's phrase for this is "data-as-schema": the content file had quietly become part of the storage format for user state. Read the "What changed" section of case study 09 to see how the new key is built, exactly which fields of a step go into it, and what the build checks so it stays unique. Then ask which kinds of content edit would still change a step's key.

excerpts.quote: ```ts /** A stable id for one step, used as the progress key. */ export function stepKey(stageId: string, moduleId: string, index: number): string { return `${stageId}/${moduleId}/${index}`; } ```
That is the hidden cost of data-as-schema: the data file had become part of the storage schema for user state, and editing content had become a schema migration without anyone deciding so.

readMore.why: stepTarget and stepKey: the single definition of today's key.

notes.title: React state updaters must be pure, and StrictMode checks
notes.body:
When you call a state setter with a function, like `setLeft((value) => ...)`, that function is an **updater**. React is allowed to call it more than once, and in development StrictMode always calls it twice on purpose, to expose code that does more than compute the next value. So an updater must be pure: take the old value, return the new one, and do nothing else (no grading, no logging, no network calls).

The postmortem in this pack is a worked example of breaking that rule. Read its root-cause section and find the guard that was supposed to stop a second grade; then work out what value that guard saw on each call.

Two more things to look at. First, how a function created during one render sees state values, compared with a `ref` (`useRef`). Second, what the app's smoke test mounts, compared with `app/src/main.tsx`, the real entry point.

excerpts.quote: 1. **Why was it graded twice?** `answer(-1)` ran twice. 2. **Why twice?** It was called from inside a `setLeft` updater. React may call updaters more than once, and StrictMode always does in development, to flush out exactly this. Updaters must be pure.

readMore.why: Root cause and contributing factors, the five whys.
The real entry point the app ships with.

notes.title: The system-design layer: one module and one question bank
notes.body:
The second half of this pack is about system design for ordinary CRUD products: the "design X" round that mid-level interviews actually run. It draws on two files in the repo.

1. **The module** (`content/modules/system-design-for-crud.md`). Read it first, top to bottom; its sections are the reading steps of this pack. It sets out the order to work in during the round (requirements, rough numbers, API, data model, read and write paths, scaling, failure modes) and walks through a Twitter-lite example.
2. **The question bank** (`content/questions/system-design-lite.json`). 140 short multiple-choice questions, each with a `why` and an `asked` note. The quizzes here come from it: caching, queues and messages, file uploads, tenants, database connections, schema changes and slow dependencies.

How to use the bank: cover the choices, answer in your own words, then compare. Read the `why` even when you were right, because it explains each wrong option too, and that is where most of the learning is. Do not trust the `answer` index on its own; a few entries point at the wrong choice, so let the `why` decide.

While reading, keep asking four questions of every design: where is the data stored, what happens if two requests arrive at the same moment, what happens if the same work is done twice, and what happens when something it depends on is slow? Then ask what each idea costs, not only what it buys.

excerpts.quote: The "design X" round at mid-level is not Netflix. It is a CRUD system with a twist: a URL shortener, a booking system, a Twitter-lite.
Caches, queues, background jobs, file storage, email, webhooks, multi-tenancy and scaling a monolith: the design round for product-engineering roles, without the FAANG theatre.

readMore.why: The system-design module: the interview structure, rough numbers, the worked example and the scaling order.
The 140-question bank the quizzes are drawn from; read the why of each question, not just the answer.

notes.title: Why unknown v1 keys are kept as they are
notes.body:
**Key: history is kept.** In `migrate()`, each old key is looked up in the frozen legacy table, and if the table has no entry the old key is used unchanged (`LEGACY[oldKey] ?? oldKey`). The decision record spells out the consequence: no step renders such a key, so it is invisible in the app, but it is still in the saved state, so it survives export and import and nothing is deleted. An earlier draft dropped these keys; F-21 records the change.

- *The build fails until each key has an entry*: no. `??` simply falls back to the old key at runtime; nothing here touches the build.
- *They count toward module completion*: no. Completion is about steps on the roadmap, and no step has that key, which is why the guide calls them invisible.
- *They are re-attached to the module's first step*: no. The code keeps the key exactly as it was; there is no re-attaching logic.

excerpts.quote: for (const [oldKey, at] of Object.entries(raw['steps'])) { if (!isNum(at)) continue; const newKey = LEGACY[oldKey] ?? oldKey; steps[newKey] = Math.max(steps[newKey] ?? 0, at);

- Bad: v1 keys the table doesn't know are kept verbatim (`LEGACY[oldKey] ?? oldKey` in `migrate`). No step renders them, so they are invisible, but they survive export and import and nothing is deleted. An earlier draft dropped them; F-21 in [loose-threads.md](../loose-threads.md) records the change. The raw v1 payload is also backed up, but nothing restores it (LT-10).

notes.title: Why the state guard did not stop the second grade
notes.body:
**Key: both calls closed over the same render's `chosen`.** The postmortem's third "why" says it directly: `answer` returned early when `chosen !== undefined`, but both calls ran inside one render, and that render's `chosen` was still `undefined`. A state value is fixed for the life of one render's closure; calling `setChosen` schedules a *new* render, it does not change the variable the second call is reading. That is why the fix adds the `answeredIndex` ref, which is read live.

- *The timer called a different answer function*: no. The guide says `answer(-1)` ran twice, the same function.
- *setChosen is asynchronous*: close in spirit, but the guide's reason is the closure: even after the update is scheduled, the current closure keeps the old value.
- *StrictMode resets state between invocations*: no. StrictMode calls the updater twice; it does not reset the component's state.

notes.title: Why the key keeps the module id
notes.body:
**Key: several modules reuse one drill deck.** The build makes `kind:target` unique *within* a module, but the same target can appear in more than one module. On the v1 roadmap 7 drill decks were used by two or three modules each; on today's roadmap 24 targets appear in more than one module (for example `drill:typescript` in four). A global `kind:target` key would make a tick in one module count for all of them, so the module must be in the key.

- *localStorage key-length limit*: the guide never mentions a length limit; the reason given is collisions.
- *Inserting a step would move ticks again*: no. Moving ticks was caused by *position* in the key. `kind:target` contains no position, with or without the module.
- *Targets repeat within one module*: the opposite. The build rejects a repeated `kind:target` inside a module.

excerpts.quote: **Why the module prefix, and why not the stage.** `kind:target` is unique within a module but not across modules. On the 2220491 roadmap, 7 drill decks were used by two or three modules each. On 2026-09-24 the same count over today's `content/roadmap.json` found 24 targets used in more than one module: 23 drill decks (for example `drill:typescript` in four modules) and one guide (`dependency-injection-explained` in two). A global `kind:target` key would merge those ticks, so the module has to be in the key. The stage does not:
export function stepKey(moduleId: string, step: Step): string { return `${moduleId}/${step.kind}:${stepTarget(step)}`; }

notes.title: What dropping the stage bought, and its price
notes.body:
**Key: modules can change stage with no key change; the build rejects duplicate module ids.** Module ids are unique across the whole roadmap, so adding the stage to the key adds no information, only fragility: moving a module to another stage would change every key in it. The case study gives the proof: three modules moved from `s6-node-backend` to `s6-backend-concepts` in the same change without touching a key. The price is that uniqueness of module ids must now be enforced, and `validateRoadmap` does that at `build-content.mjs:299-303`.

- *Faster lookups, by forbidding shared decks*: modules still share decks; that is why the module stays in the key.
- *No functional gain*: there is one, stage moves are free.
- *Shorter keys, with a migration on stage rename*: dropping the stage is exactly what removes the need for a migration when a module changes stage.

excerpts.quote: merge those ticks, so the module has to be in the key. The stage does not: module ids are unique across the whole roadmap, so the stage adds no information, and including it would make moving a module between stages break every key in it. The roadmap review made that call to drop the stage prefix, and three modules (`m-rest-api`, `m-sql`, `m-auth`) moved from `s6-node-backend` to `s6-backend-concepts` in the same change without touching a single key.

notes.title: Why the legacy key map must never be regenerated
notes.body:
**Key: old ticks follow the 2220491 roadmap's positions.** A v1 key like `stage/module/3` only means something in the roadmap that v1 shipped with: "the step at index 3 of that module, as it was then". The legacy table translates those old positions into new keys. If you regenerated it from today's edited roadmap, index 3 might now be a different step, so old ticks would be sent to the wrong place. That is why the generator refuses to overwrite its output without `--force`: "a regenerated map would describe the new roadmap, not the one old progress was written against."

- *It edits roadmap.json in place*: the guard is about the generator's output file; nothing says it edits the roadmap.
- *A second run doubles each entry*: the guard stops a second run from overwriting the file; nothing suggests it would append duplicates.
- *Noisy diff*: a cosmetic worry; the real harm is wrong mappings.

excerpts.quote: ([F-20](../loose-threads.md)). It checks each override exists and keeps its kind (`:64-71`) and refuses to overwrite its output without `--force` (`:48-51`), because a regenerated map would describe the new roadmap, not the one old progress was written against. `migrate()` in `progress.ts`

notes.title: Why migration uses a frozen table, not the live roadmap
notes.body:
**Key: rekeying would read old positions through the new roadmap, which also loads after progress.** Two facts from the decision record combine here. First, `progress.ts` loads synchronously when it is imported, but the roadmap arrives later by `fetch`, so a migration that needs the roadmap cannot run inside `read()`. Second, and worse, option (a) would interpret *old* positions using the *new* roadmap, which is "exactly wrong once the roadmap has been edited". The frozen table already knows what each old position meant, so `migrate()` only needs the data's shape.

- *There is no server*: the content is fetched; the problem is timing and meaning, not a missing server.
- *ContentGate renders on each navigation*: the guide does not give this as the reason.
- *The table ships smaller*: the opposite; its listed cost is a 14,919-byte JSON file in the bundle.

excerpts.quote: - `progress.ts` loads synchronously at import time. The content (and so the roadmap) arrives later, by `fetch`. Any migration that needs the roadmap cannot run inside `read()`.

- **(a) Rekey at load time against the current roadmap**, in `ContentGate` after content arrives. Cost: couples progress to content. Worse, it reads *old positions* through the *new* roadmap, which is exactly wrong once the roadmap has been edited. - **(b) A table generated once from the 2220491 roadmap, frozen**, applied by a shape-only `migrate()` that needs no content. Cost: a 14,919-byte JSON file in the bundle (`wc -c app/src/lib/legacy-step-keys.json`), and a generator that must never be re-run.

notes.title: What the backup-then-write order in read() guarantees
notes.body:
**Key: the first raw v1 payload stays the rollback copy, and reloads read v2 directly.** Look at the two lines inside `read()`. The backup is written only if `V1_BACKUP_KEY` is still empty, so the very first untouched v1 string is the one kept. Then the migrated state is written straight back under the normal key. On the next load the stored data says version 2, so neither the migration nor the backup runs again, as the code comment says. If the write fails, the in-memory state is still correct and the next commit retries.

- *Each reload refreshes the backup*: no, the `=== null` check prevents overwriting it.
- *Both versions stay live and the newer is read*: the app reads only the main key; the decision record notes nothing restores the backup (LT-10).
- *Written after the learner confirms a prompt*: there is no prompt; the write happens immediately in `read()`.

excerpts.quote: // The untouched v1 payload stays around as the rollback path, and the // migrated state is written straight back so a reload doesn't migrate // (or back up) again. if (localStorage.getItem(V1_BACKUP_KEY) === null) localStorage.setItem(V1_BACKUP_KEY, raw); localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(next));

notes.title: Why adding tags to a drill orphans its ticks
notes.body:
**Key: orphaned, because tags are part of the target.** `stepTarget` returns `deck|tags` for a drill with tags, so adding a `tags` array changes the target and therefore the step key. Every learner's tick sits on the old key, which no step renders any more. Nothing complains: the coverage test in `selectors.test.ts` only checks the values of the frozen v1 table, and this step was created after v2, so its key is one of the 88 unguarded ones (LT-15).

- *Unaffected, tags are metadata*: the code puts the tags into the target string.
- *Ticks move to an untagged twin*: a key change does not transfer ticks anywhere; they are simply left behind.
- *migrate() rekeys on each load*: `migrate()` returns the data unchanged unless `version` is 1, and it only knows the frozen v1 table.

excerpts.quote: case 'drill': return step.tags?.length ? `${step.deck}|${step.tags.join(',')}` : step.deck;

step's target in place. Swap a drill's deck, point a build at a different project, fix a read step's anchor, or change a drill's tags (tags are part of the target), and the step gets a new key. Every learner's tick on the old key is orphaned, silently, in every browser. The coverage test only protects the 195 keys in the v1 table; 88 of today's 283 keys were minted since, and nothing protects them. `js/86-sqlite-orders` in `m-sql` is one of them.

notes.title: Why the build imports stepTarget instead of copying it
notes.body:
**Key: so the uniqueness check runs on the exact key the app stores.** `validateRoadmap` builds `kind:target` with `stepTarget(step)` for each step and reports a repeat within a module. If the build had its own copy of the target rule, the two could drift: the build might think two steps differ while the app gives them the same key, and two steps would share one tick without anyone noticing. The case study states it: the build imports `stepTarget` from `types.ts` "so the build validates the exact key the app stores".

- *The JSON is parsed through types.ts types*: TypeScript types do not exist at runtime; the import is for the function.
- *Faster build by reusing a compiled bundle*: the script imports the source file, not a bundle, and the guide's reason is correctness.
- *A .mjs script cannot switch over unions*: `stepTarget` is an ordinary switch on `step.kind`; any JavaScript can do that.

excerpts.quote: import { stepTarget } from '../app/src/lib/types.ts';
const key = `${step.kind}:${stepTarget(step)}`; if (targets.has(key)) problems.push(`${where}: two steps are both "${key}"`);
within a module (`:307-309`). `build-content.mjs` imports `stepTarget` from `types.ts` (`:22`) so the build validates the exact key the app stores.

notes.title: What counting against a fixed deadline fixes
notes.body:
**Key: drift.** Browsers throttle timers in background tabs, so an interval set for 250 ms may fire much later. If the countdown subtracts one per tick, a slow tab makes the clock run slow. The rewritten `Countdown` instead stores `deadline` once and compares `Date.now()` against it on every tick, so however late a tick arrives, the time shown is right. The postmortem lists this as a contributing factor: the deadline-free design "let a throttled background tab drift".

- *Leaked intervals*: the new version clears its interval in the effect cleanup; that is not what the deadline changes.
- *Timezone or midnight errors*: `Date.now()` is a plain millisecond count, unaffected by time zones; the guide does not mention this.
- *Wasted renders*: the new version still calls `setNow` every tick, so it renders just as often.

const id = setInterval(() => { const t = Date.now(); setNow(t); if (t >= deadline && !fired.current) {
5. **Contributing:** counting ticks inside the updater mixed "what time is it" with "what happens when time runs out". The deadline-free design also let a throttled background tab drift.

notes.title: What inserting a step did under the v1 index key
notes.body:
**Key: each tick slides one step.** The v1 key ends in the step's index. After inserting a step at position 1, the new step sits at index 1, so it shows whatever tick was stored under `.../1` (old step 1's). Every later step has moved down one index, so each stored tick now lands on the step before the one it was earned on. No error is raised, and it happens in every learner's browser at once.

- *The build fails on a duplicate index*: indexes are just positions in a list, so they never collide, and the guide says none of this throws.
- *The new step is unticked and the rest stay put*: that is what a content-derived key gives you, not an index key.
- *Ticks are cleared because the count changed*: stored ticks are not cleared; they stay and are reinterpreted.

excerpts.quote: export function stepKey(stageId: string, moduleId: string, index: number): string { return `${stageId}/${moduleId}/${index}`; }

Insert a step at position 1 of a module, and the new step inherits the tick stored under `.../1`; every later tick in that module slides onto the step before the one it was earned on. notes.title: Cache-aside versus write-through: when data enters the cache
notes.body:
**Key: cache-aside fills the cache on a read miss; write-through updates the cache on every write.** The difference is *when* data gets into the cache. With cache-aside, the application asks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database, stores the result and returns it. So only data that someone actually reads is cached, and an entry stays stale until it is deleted or its TTL runs out. With write-through, every write updates the store and the cache together, so the cache is always fresh, but it also fills up with rows nobody ever reads.

- *Separate server versus inside the database*: where the cache runs is a deployment choice; both patterns usually sit in front of the same Redis.
- *Never expires versus expires when the row changes*: both can use TTLs; expiry is not what separates them.
- *Buffers writes and flushes them in batches*: that is a third pattern, write-behind. It is fast, but writes still in the buffer are lost if the cache dies.

excerpts.quote: Cache-aside loads lazily, so it only caches what is read, and entries go stale until invalidated or expired. Write-through keeps the cache fresh on every write, at the cost of caching data nobody reads. Buffering writes for later is write-behind, a third pattern.

notes.title: Stopping a cache stampede: one rebuild instead of five hundred
notes.body:
**Key: let one request rebuild the value while the others wait for it or get the stale copy.** A stampede happens because every request that misses goes to the database at once. If 500 requests arrive in the second after a popular key expires, 500 identical queries hit the database. Coalescing (a per-key lock, or single-flight) lets the first miss run the query while the other 499 wait for its result or are served the old value until the new one lands: 1 query instead of 500. Refreshing a little early, with random jitter so keys do not all expire together, avoids the miss in the first place.

- *Longer TTL*: the key expires less often, but when it does, all 500 requests still miss together. Rarer, not smaller.
- *Shorter TTL*: more expiries, and each burst is still as big as the traffic that arrives during the miss.
- *Read replica*: the same 500 queries are split over two databases, about 250 each. Halved, not solved.

excerpts.quote: Request coalescing (a lock or single-flight per key), serving stale while one caller refreshes, or refreshing early with jitter all make one query do the work of hundreds. A longer TTL only makes the stampede rarer; a replica halves it.

notes.title: Why a CDN served one user's orders to another user
notes.body:
**Key: a per-user response was cacheable by shared caches; it needs `private` or `no-store`.** A shared cache such as a CDN stores a response under its URL. `/api/me/orders` is the same URL for every logged-in user, because the user is identified by a cookie or token, not by the path. So the first response stored is handed to the next person who asks for that URL. `Cache-Control: private` means only the user's own browser may keep a copy; `no-store` means nobody may.

- *The TTL was too long*: with a 30-second TTL the same stored copy still goes to everyone who asks in those 30 seconds. It only leaks for less time.
- *Edge servers share a disk*: the storage layout is not the issue; the CDN did exactly what the response headers allowed.
- *Matching ETags swapped responses*: an ETag lets a cache check whether the copy it already holds is still current. It never decides whose response to serve.

excerpts.quote: Shared caches key on the URL, and `/me/orders` is the same URL for everyone. Personal responses must say `Cache-Control: private` (browser only) or `no-store`. A short TTL just leaks for less time.

notes.title: Why update code deletes the cache key instead of setting it
notes.body:
**Key: two concurrent writers can set the cache out of order, leaving an old value in place.** Walk through it. Writer A saves a price of 10; writer B then saves 12, so the database ends at 12. Each writer then sets the cache. Network timing means A's set can arrive after B's, so the cache now says 10 while the database says 12, and it stays wrong until the TTL expires. If both writers delete the key instead, the order of the two deletes does not matter: the key is gone either way, and the next read fetches 12 from the database.

- *Deleting is faster than overwriting*: the two cost about the same in Redis; speed is not the reason.
- *Writing would need a distributed transaction*: neither approach uses one; the problem is the order of two writes, not atomicity.
- *A deleted key gets a fresh TTL*: a set can carry a TTL just as easily.

excerpts.quote: If writer A and writer B both update the row and then set the cache, A's set can land after B's and leave A's older value cached indefinitely. Deleting lets the next read fetch whatever the database holds now.

notes.title: Duplicate charges from an at-least-once queue
notes.body:
**Key: make the consumer idempotent, for example by recording processed message ids.** At-least-once means a message can arrive twice: the consumer charges the card, crashes before acknowledging, and the queue delivers the message again. You cannot prevent that, so make the second delivery harmless. Record each message id in a table with a unique key (if the insert fails, it was already done: skip), or pass an idempotency key to the payment provider so it refuses a second charge. At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer gives effectively-once effects.

- *Exactly-once mode*: no setting removes every duplicate end to end; brokers that advertise it mean deduplication within a time window, or inside their own system.
- *Acknowledge before processing*: that is at-most-once. A crash after the ack loses the charge completely.
- *Delay each charge*: a delay cannot tell which copy is the duplicate, and nothing guarantees the order in which the copies arrive.

excerpts.quote: At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer gives effectively-once effects: store the message id (or pass an idempotency key to the payment provider) and skip repeats. Acknowledging first turns it into at-most-once, so a crash loses the charge.

notes.title: The transactional outbox: saving the order and its event together
notes.body:
**Key: save the event in an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes it later.** The problem is a dual write: the database and the broker are two systems with no shared transaction, so a crash between the two leaves one without the other. The outbox puts the event row in the *same* database transaction as the order, so both commit or neither does. A separate relay reads unpublished outbox rows, publishes them and marks them done, retrying until the broker accepts. If it crashes after publishing but before marking a row, it publishes that row again, which is why consumers must still be idempotent.

- *Publish first, save after*: moves the gap. If the save then fails, an event exists for an order that does not.
- *Two-phase commit*: a distributed transaction across database and broker is exactly what the outbox avoids; most brokers do not support it.
- *Retry the publish in a loop inside the request*: the loop dies with the process, which is the failure in the question.

excerpts.quote: The order and its event commit or roll back together, and a separate relay reads the outbox and publishes, retrying until it succeeds. Consumers may see a duplicate, so they stay idempotent.

notes.title: A poison message: cap the retries, then dead-letter it
notes.body:
**Key: cap delivery attempts, then move the message to a dead-letter queue and alert.** A poison message can never succeed, for example one with malformed JSON: every redelivery fails the same way. Capping attempts (say five, with backoff between them) still gives a transient failure such as a timeout a fair chance. After the cap, the message moves to a dead-letter queue, where it no longer blocks the queue or wastes capacity but is kept for a person to inspect. The alert matters: a dead-letter queue nobody watches is just a bin.

- *Retry forever with backoff*: the fault is in the message or the code, so retries cannot fix it; they burn capacity and, on an ordered queue, hold up everything behind it.
- *Delete it on the first failure*: also throws away messages that failed only for a transient reason.
- *Restart the consumer after each failure*: the message is unchanged, so the next delivery fails the same way.

excerpts.quote: A poison message never succeeds, so unbounded retries waste capacity and can block ordered queues. Capping attempts and dead-lettering keeps the message for diagnosis.

notes.title: Keeping one order's events in sequence without losing parallelism
notes.body:
**Key: partition by order id, so every event for one order reaches the same consumer in order.** Ordering only matters *within* one order: for order 42, OrderPlaced must be handled before OrderCancelled, but orders 42 and 43 do not care about each other. Partitioning by order id (Kafka partitions, SQS FIFO message groups, Service Bus sessions) sends all of order 42's events to one consumer, in sequence, while other orders run on other consumers in parallel.

- *One consumer for the whole queue*: keeps order, but throws away the parallelism; ten consumers' worth of work now runs on one.
- *Timestamps and sleeping*: a consumer cannot know whether an earlier event is still in flight, and clocks on different machines disagree.
- *Let any consumer take any event, sort later*: too late. A handler has already acted on the cancellation of an order it has not seen placed.

excerpts.quote: Ordering is needed per key, not globally, so partitioning by key (Kafka partitions, SQS FIFO message groups, Service Bus sessions) keeps parallelism across orders. A single consumer works but throws away all throughput.

notes.title: What a 30-second visibility timeout does to a 45-second job
notes.body:
**Key: the message becomes visible again and a second consumer processes it too.** When a consumer receives an SQS message, the message is hidden, not removed. The consumer must delete it before the visibility timeout ends; otherwise the broker assumes the consumer died and shows the message again. Timeline: at second 0 consumer A receives it; at second 30 the timeout ends and consumer B receives it; at second 45 A finishes; at second 75 B finishes. One message, processed twice, and nothing failed. Fix: a timeout longer than the slowest job (or extend it while working), plus an idempotent consumer.

- *The broker cancels the work*: the broker cannot stop your code; it can only hand the message out again.
- *Straight to the dead-letter queue*: dead-lettering happens after repeated receives reach a maximum count, not after one timeout.
- *Only applies before the first delivery*: the timeout starts again at every receive.

excerpts.quote: While a consumer works, the message is hidden; if it is not deleted before the timeout, the broker assumes the consumer died and delivers it again. The fix is a longer timeout or extending it while working, plus idempotency.

notes.title: Keeping 2 GB uploads off your API servers
notes.body:
**Key: the API hands out a short-lived pre-signed URL; the browser uploads straight to storage.** The API's job shrinks to two small requests: check that the user may upload, then sign a URL that allows one write to one object key for a few minutes. The browser sends the 2 GB straight to object storage, then tells the API the upload finished so it can record the key. Your servers never touch the bytes.

- *Stream into a binary column in the database*: every byte passes through the API, and the database grows by 2 GB per video, which slows its backups and replicas too.
- *Raise the body limit and scale out*: it works, but all 2 GB of every upload still flows through your servers, and you pay for that capacity.
- *Chunk in the browser and post the chunks to the API*: the chunks still go through your API; splitting the bytes does not send them anywhere else.

excerpts.quote: A pre-signed URL grants time-limited permission to write one object, so the bytes go from browser to object storage while your API only authorises and records the key. Chunking through the API still pushes every byte through your servers.
never goes through your API: the client uploads straight to object storage with a presigned URL, and a CDN serves it.

notes.title: Cleaning up abandoned uploads without deleting real files
notes.body:
**Key: write uploads under a `pending/` prefix and let a lifecycle rule expire them.** With direct uploads, the file reaches storage before your API knows whether the user will finish. Put every new upload under `pending/`. When the user confirms, copy or move it to its final key. A bucket lifecycle rule then deletes anything still under `pending/` after, say, one day. Storage does the clean-up itself, and it only ever touches files that were never confirmed.

- *A monthly job that deletes any object older than thirty days*: age does not tell you whether a file was confirmed, so this deletes real files too.
- *Delete when the browser tab closes*: a crash, a flat battery or a dropped connection sends nothing, so the browser cannot be relied on.
- *Public URLs so users clean up*: makes every file readable by anyone, and users will not tidy up anyway.

excerpts.quote: Unconfirmed uploads land under a temporary prefix; confirming copies or moves them to their final key, and a bucket lifecycle rule deletes anything left in `pending/` after a day.

notes.title: One tenant's export slowing every tenant: isolate the workload
notes.body:
**Key: per-tenant quotas and rate limits, with heavy exports moved to a queue and a replica.** The problem is not total capacity; it is one tenant's batch job competing with everyone's interactive requests on the same primary database. Throttle per tenant, so nobody can take more than a fair share, and run exports as background jobs that read from a replica. Interactive traffic keeps the primary, and the export runs as fast as the replica allows. Very large tenants may eventually move to a database of their own.

- *A larger database instance*: you pay all month for one tenant's nightly peak, and the next, bigger export saturates it again.
- *An index on tenant_id*: helps filtering, but does not limit how much CPU and disk one tenant's export can use.
- *Separate login pages per tenant*: changes how requests arrive, not where they run; every query still hits the same database.

excerpts.quote: Isolate the heavy workload: throttle per tenant, and run exports as background jobs against a replica so they cannot starve interactive traffic. A bigger instance buys time until the next export grows.

notes.title: Where the email uniqueness rule goes in a shared-schema app
notes.body:
**Key: `UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)` on the users table.** In a shared-schema app every tenant's users sit in one table, told apart by `tenant_id`. The rule is "unique within a tenant", so the constraint covers the pair. Example: alice@example.com works with two customer companies. The rows (tenant 1, alice) and (tenant 2, alice) are both allowed; a second (tenant 1, alice) is rejected.

- *`UNIQUE (email)` across the whole table*: rejects Alice's second company, because her email already exists for tenant 1.
- *`UNIQUE (tenant_id)`*: allows exactly one user per tenant, so the second person to join a company fails.
- *No constraint, check in the API*: two sign-ups at the same moment both look, both find nothing, and both insert. A constraint makes the check and the insert one step inside the database.

excerpts.quote: The same person may belong to two customer organisations, so email is unique within a tenant, not globally.

notes.title: Why 40 app instances overwhelmed Postgres, and what fixes it
notes.body:
**Key: put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front of Postgres and shrink each app pool.** Do the arithmetic: 4 instances × 50 connections was 200; 40 × 50 is 2,000. Each Postgres connection is its own server process with its own memory, and most of those 2,000 sit idle at any moment. A pooler accepts all the client connections and multiplexes them onto a small number of real server connections, handing one out only for the length of a transaction. Smaller app pools keep the total sensible as you add instances.

- *Raise `max_connections` to 2,000*: Postgres can be told to accept them, but 2,000 processes, mostly idle, still cost memory and hurt performance.
- *Remove the app-side pools*: every request then pays to open and close a connection, which is slower and still unbounded under load.
- *Add a read replica*: it only takes reads, and each instance still opens its full pool.

excerpts.quote: Each Postgres connection is a process with its own memory, so thousands of mostly idle connections hurt performance. A pooler multiplexes many client connections onto a few server ones. Dropping app pools makes it worse, and a replica only helps reads.

notes.title: Renaming a column while old and new code both run
notes.body:
**Key: add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old one.** During a rolling deploy, some instances run the old code, which uses `fullname`, and some run the new code. Every schema state must work for both. The sequence: (1) add `display_name`; (2) deploy code that writes both columns; (3) copy existing rows across in batches; (4) switch reads to `display_name`; (5) once no running version uses `fullname`, drop it. Each step is compatible with the code on either side of it. This is expand and contract.

- *Rename in one migration, then deploy*: old instances still query `fullname` and fail the moment the rename runs.
- *Deploy first, then rename*: new instances query `display_name` before it exists and fail.
- *Five minutes offline*: works, but avoiding exactly that is why rolling deploys exist.

excerpts.quote: Expand and contract keeps the schema compatible with both app versions at every step. Renaming first breaks the old instances still reading `fullname`; deploying first breaks the new ones.

notes.title: What a circuit breaker adds when retries make an outage worse
notes.body:
**Key: after repeated failures it fails fast for a cool-off period instead of calling.** A breaker counts recent failures for one dependency. Closed: calls go through. Once failures pass a threshold it opens, and calls fail immediately, without touching the struggling service, for a cool-off period. Then it goes half-open and lets a trial call through; success closes it, failure opens it again. The struggling service gets room to recover, and your own threads stop waiting on timeouts.

- *Retries each failed call straight away, several times*: that is the problem in the question. With four retries, every caller sends up to five requests where one would do.
- *Raises the timeout*: each stuck call then holds a thread even longer.
- *Routes to a cached copy on the calling side*: a fallback you might add next to a breaker, but not what a breaker does.

excerpts.quote: Once failures pass a threshold the breaker opens and calls fail immediately, then a trial call tests recovery. That stops your retries from piling onto a struggling service and frees your own threads.

notes.title: Containing one slow dependency with a bulkhead
notes.body:
**Key: a bulkhead, a separate capped pool for calls to that API.** Say the service has 200 worker threads and the slow API now takes 30 seconds to answer. Without a limit, requests that call it keep arriving until all 200 threads are waiting on it, and requests that never touch it find no thread free. A bulkhead caps calls to that API at, say, 10 at a time. When it slows, those 10 fill up and that one feature queues or fails, while the other 190 threads keep serving everything else. The name comes from the walls in a ship's hull that stop one leak flooding every compartment.

- *A larger global thread pool*: 400 threads fill up the same way, just a little later.
- *A read replica*: moves database reads; the problem is outbound API calls.
- *Sticky sessions*: decide which server a user lands on, and do nothing about threads waiting on another service.

excerpts.quote: A bulkhead limits how many concurrent calls may go to one dependency, so when it slows down only that feature queues or fails and the rest of the service keeps its capacity. A bigger pool fills up too, just later.
What happens when a dependency is slow, or two requests race.

notes.title: Making a double-clicked "Place order" safe on the server
notes.body:
**Key: accept an `Idempotency-Key` header and replay the first response.** The client generates one unique key per checkout attempt and sends it with the request and with every retry of it. The server stores the key alongside the result. When the second request arrives with the same key, the server does not create another order; it returns the stored response from the first one. One order, one charge, and both requests get the same answer.

- *Reject any second order from the same customer within a minute*: blocks a customer who really does order twice, and still only guesses what a duplicate is.
- *Disable the button and rely on the client*: a good extra, but it lives in the browser; a network retry or a replayed request bypasses it.
- *A nightly job that compares baskets*: runs after the card has already been charged twice.

excerpts.quote: The client generates a key per checkout attempt; the server stores it with the result and returns the stored result for any repeat.
an idempotency key on the POST.
